claim: Single-neuron genomics enables direct measurement of somatic mutation rates in human brain.
source: Single-neuron genomics enables direct measurement of somatic mutation rates in human brain and promises to answer this question.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a capability of the technology.

claim: The reanalysis supports a mutation frequency of approximately 0.2 events per cell.
source: Our reanalysis supports a mutation frequency of approximately 0.2 events per cell, which is about fifty-fold lower than reported, confirming that L1 elements mobilize in some human neurons but indicating that L1 mosaicism is not ubiquitous.
evidence: This is based on the authors' reanalysis of the Upton et al. data, as detailed in the Results section.

claim: The corrected mutation frequency is about fifty-fold lower than reported by Upton et al.
source: Our reanalysis supports a mutation frequency of approximately 0.2 events per cell, which is about fifty-fold lower than reported, confirming that L1 elements mobilize in some human neurons but indicating that L1 mosaicism is not ubiquitous.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the reanalysis results to the original Upton et al. findings.

claim: L1 elements mobilize in some human neurons.
source: Our reanalysis supports a mutation frequency of approximately 0.2 events per cell, which is about fifty-fold lower than reported, confirming that L1 elements mobilize in some human neurons but indicating that L1 mosaicism is not ubiquitous.
evidence: This is confirmed by the reanalysis showing a low but non-zero rate of L1 mobilization.

claim: L1 mosaicism is not ubiquitous.
source: Our reanalysis supports a mutation frequency of approximately 0.2 events per cell, which is about fifty-fold lower than reported, confirming that L1 elements mobilize in some human neurons but indicating that L1 mosaicism is not ubiquitous.
evidence: This is inferred from the low rate of L1 mobilization found in the reanalysis.

claim: LINE-1 (L1) elements are endogenous retrotransposons that transcribe an RNA copy that is reverse-transcribed into a DNA copy that can then insert into a novel site in the genome.
source: LINE-1 (L1) elements are endogenous retrotransposons that transcribe an RNA copy that is reverse-transcribed into a DNA copy that can then insert into a novel site in the genome, creating mutations capable of disrupting or modifying the expression of genes in which they insert or neighboring genes (Goodier and Kazazian, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about L1 elements, supported by citation.

claim: L1 insertions can create mutations capable of disrupting or modifying the expression of genes in which they insert or neighboring genes.
source: LINE-1 (L1) elements are endogenous retrotransposons that transcribe an RNA copy that is reverse-transcribed into a DNA copy that can then insert into a novel site in the genome, creating mutations capable of disrupting or modifying the expression of genes in which they insert or neighboring genes (Goodier and Kazazian, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about L1 elements, supported by citation.

claim: Transposon mobilization is an essential cause of the generation of species diversity.
source: Evolutionarily, transposon mobilization is an essential cause of the generation of species diversity (Cordaux and Batzer, 2009), so interest in possible L1 activity during brain development was spurred by the discovery that these elements can mobilize in neuronal progenitor cells (Coufal et al., 2009; Muotri et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cordaux and Batzer, 2009.

claim: L1 elements can mobilize in neuronal progenitor cells.
source: Evolutionarily, transposon mobilization is an essential cause of the generation of species diversity (Cordaux and Batzer, 2009), so interest in possible L1 activity during brain development was spurred by the discovery that these elements can mobilize in neuronal progenitor cells (Coufal et al., 2009; Muotri et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coufal et al., 2009 and Muotri et al., 2005.

claim: Single-cell sequencing has revealed and quantified previously unknown mechanisms of somatic mutation in the human brain.
source: Single-cell sequencing is a powerful technology that has revealed and quantified previously unknown mechanisms of somatic mutation in the human brain, providing a first proof of principle for the systematic measurement of somatic mutation rates in any normal human tissue (Evrony et al., 2012; McConnell et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2014; Evrony et al., 2015; Lodato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior single-cell sequencing studies.

claim: Single-cell sequencing provides a first proof of principle for the systematic measurement of somatic mutation rates in any normal human tissue.
source: Single-cell sequencing is a powerful technology that has revealed and quantified previously unknown mechanisms of somatic mutation in the human brain, providing a first proof of principle for the systematic measurement of somatic mutation rates in any normal human tissue (Evrony et al., 2012; McConnell et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2014; Evrony et al., 2015; Lodato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior single-cell sequencing studies.

claim: L1 mobilization has been observed at low rates using a transgenic L1 reporter in rodent brain in vivo.
source: L1 mobilization has been observed at low rates using indirect genetic techniques such as a transgenic L1 reporter in rodent brain in vivo (Muotri et al., 2005; 2010) and human progenitor cells in vitro (Coufal et al., 2009), while studies profiling human brain bulk DNA suggested much higher rates (Baillie et al., 2011; Bundo et al., 2014; Coufal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Muotri et al., 2005 and 2010.

claim: L1 mobilization has been observed at low rates in human progenitor cells in vitro.
source: L1 mobilization has been observed at low rates using indirect genetic techniques such as a transgenic L1 reporter in rodent brain in vivo (Muotri et al., 2005; 2010) and human progenitor cells in vitro (Coufal et al., 2009), while studies profiling human brain bulk DNA suggested much higher rates (Baillie et al., 2011; Bundo et al., 2014; Coufal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coufal et al., 2009.

claim: Studies profiling human brain bulk DNA suggested much higher rates of L1 mobilization.
source: L1 mobilization has been observed at low rates using indirect genetic techniques such as a transgenic L1 reporter in rodent brain in vivo (Muotri et al., 2005; 2010) and human progenitor cells in vitro (Coufal et al., 2009), while studies profiling human brain bulk DNA suggested much higher rates (Baillie et al., 2011; Bundo et al., 2014; Coufal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baillie et al., 2011; Bundo et al., 2014; Coufal et al., 2009.

claim: Single-cell sequencing has been proposed as the definitive method to resolve disparate estimates of L1 mobilization rates.
source: Single-cell sequencing has been proposed as the definitive method to resolve these disparate estimates (Erwin et al., 2014; Goodier, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Erwin et al., 2014 and Goodier, 2014.

claim: More than half (7 of 13) of Upton et al.'s putative PCR-validated candidates are chimera artifacts.
source: Sequence analysis of Upton et al.'s putative PCR-validated candidates (Table S2 of Upton et al.) demonstrates that more than half of them (7 of 13) are chimera artifacts that could not have been generated by the process of L1 mobilization (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on the authors' sequence analysis of the candidates, documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Some chimeras originated immediately downstream of germline L1Hs/L1Pa elements that are incapable of retrotransposition because the L1 elements are truncated, are from an old, inactive L1 subfamily, or contain numerous inactivating mutations.
source: Some chimeras originated immediately downstream of germline L1Hs/L1Pa elements that are incapable of retrotransposition, because the L1 elements are truncated, are from an old, inactive L1 subfamily, or contain numerous inactivating mutations (Figure 1B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: In some cases, L1 5' and 3' junction chimeras originating from distinct L1 elements were misinterpreted as two ends of the same L1.
source: In other cases, L1 5' and 3' junction chimeras originating from distinct L1 elements were misinterpreted as two ends of the same L1 (Figures 1B–C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figures 1B-C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Some candidates lack poly-A tails, a key feature of retrotransposon insertions.
source: Some candidates lack poly-A tails (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1), a key feature of retrotransposon insertions.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Upton et al. performed 3' junction PCR validation for 10 RC-seq candidates for which they had detected the 5'end, and 3' junction validation failed for all 10.
source: Upton et al. performed 3' junction PCR validation for 10 RC-seq candidates for which they had detected the 5'end, and while 3' junction validation is technically straightforward, it failed for all 10.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the validation results from Upton et al.

claim: Poly-A tails do not obstruct PCR.
source: Whereas the authors attribute their validation failure to poly-A tails obstructing PCR amplification, poly-A tails do not obstruct PCR: the single-cell RC-seq method used by Upton et al. itself entails three PCR steps in which L1 3' junctions are amplified, and 3' junction PCR is the standard validation approach used in L1 studies (Ewing and Kazazian, 2010; Grandi et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2010; Iskow et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to standard L1 studies and by the fact that the RC-seq method itself uses PCR on 3' junctions.

claim: 3' junction PCR is the standard validation approach used in L1 studies.
source: Whereas the authors attribute their validation failure to poly-A tails obstructing PCR amplification, poly-A tails do not obstruct PCR: the single-cell RC-seq method used by Upton et al. itself entails three PCR steps in which L1 3' junctions are amplified, and 3' junction PCR is the standard validation approach used in L1 studies (Ewing and Kazazian, 2010; Grandi et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2010; Iskow et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple L1 studies.

claim: The failure of all 10/10 3' junction validation attempts suggests a high prevalence of false-positives among RC-seq candidates detected with only 5' junction reads.
source: The failure of all 10/10 3' junction validation attempts suggests a high prevalence of false-positives among RC-seq candidates detected with only 5' junction reads, which represent 27% of all candidate insertions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the validation failure rate.

claim: Candidates detected with only 5' junction reads represent 27% of all candidate insertions in Upton et al.
source: The failure of all 10/10 3' junction validation attempts suggests a high prevalence of false-positives among RC-seq candidates detected with only 5' junction reads, which represent 27% of all candidate insertions.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the composition of candidates in Upton et al.

claim: A bona fide L1 insertion creates two genome breakpoints at the insertion site, one on each end of the insertion (5' and 3').
source: A bona fide L1 insertion creates two genome breakpoints at the insertion site, one on each end of the insertion (5' and 3'), while a chimera has only one breakpoint at the called insertion site (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about L1 insertions, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: A chimera has only one breakpoint at the called insertion site.
source: A bona fide L1 insertion creates two genome breakpoints at the insertion site, one on each end of the insertion (5' and 3'), while a chimera has only one breakpoint at the called insertion site (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about chimeras, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Full-length cloning validation is the only way to confirm that both breakpoints are present in the same DNA molecule as a bona fide insertion.
source: Full-length cloning validation, in which the entire L1 insertion is amplified in a single DNA molecule spanning both breakpoints (using primers based in the genomic sequence flanking the L1), is therefore the only way to confirm that both breakpoints are present in the same DNA molecule as a bona fide insertion, as opposed to two different chimeric molecules (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a logical inference about validation methods, illustrated in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upton et al. did not perform full-length cloning validation on any insertion.
source: However, Upton et al. did not perform full-length cloning validation on any insertion.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the methods used by Upton et al.

claim: Two independent chimeras can occur by chance in two different DNA molecules/copies whose non-L1 sequences overlap the same genomic locus, giving the false appearance of a target site duplication (TSD).
source: Two independent chimeras can even occur by chance in two different DNA molecules/copies whose non-L1 sequences overlap the same genomic locus, giving the false appearance of a target site duplication (TSD) (Figures 1B–C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by examples in Figures 1B-C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: MALBAC produces short amplicons (0.5–1.5kb) compared to multiple displacement amplification (MDA) (10–50 kb amplicons).
source: MALBAC produces short amplicons (0.5–1.5kb) compared to multiple displacement amplification (MDA) (10–50 kb amplicons) (Dean et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2015; Zong et al., 2012), so insertions longer than ~1.5 kb (~15–30% of somatic L1 insertions in human cancer studies [Helman et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2012; Tubio et al., 2014]) would not be efficiently validated in MALBAC single cells (Figure 1—figure supplements 1A and C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing MALBAC and MDA.

claim: Insertions longer than ~1.5 kb (~15–30% of somatic L1 insertions in human cancer studies) would not be efficiently validated in MALBAC single cells.
source: MALBAC produces short amplicons (0.5–1.5kb) compared to multiple displacement amplification (MDA) (10–50 kb amplicons) (Dean et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2015; Zong et al., 2012), so insertions longer than ~1.5 kb (~15–30% of somatic L1 insertions in human cancer studies [Helman et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2012; Tubio et al., 2014]) would not be efficiently validated in MALBAC single cells (Figure 1—figure supplements 1A and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on MALBAC amplicon size and the size distribution of L1 insertions from cancer studies.

claim: One recurrent type of chimera artifact accounts for 16% of Upton et al.'s candidates detected only at a 5' junction.
source: Furthermore, even some chimeras that can be identified computationally were not filtered: one recurrent type of chimera artifact accounts for 16% of their candidates detected only at a 5' junction (Supplementary file 1; see example candidate chr11:112602973).
evidence: This is based on the authors' analysis documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: 97% (4634/4759) of Upton et al.'s single-cell insertion calls were supported by a single Illumina sequencing read.
source: As a result, 97% (4634/4759) of their single-cell insertion calls were supported by a single Illumina sequencing read and 99.6% by 1 or 2 reads; 94% of their >320,000 candidates from 'bulk' DNA were also supported by only 1 read (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the read count data from Upton et al., shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 99.6% of Upton et al.'s single-cell insertion calls were supported by 1 or 2 reads.
source: As a result, 97% (4634/4759) of their single-cell insertion calls were supported by a single Illumina sequencing read and 99.6% by 1 or 2 reads; 94% of their >320,000 candidates from 'bulk' DNA were also supported by only 1 read (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the read count data from Upton et al., shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 94% of Upton et al.'s >320,000 candidates from 'bulk' DNA were supported by only 1 read.
source: As a result, 97% (4634/4759) of their single-cell insertion calls were supported by a single Illumina sequencing read and 99.6% by 1 or 2 reads; 94% of their >320,000 candidates from 'bulk' DNA were also supported by only 1 read (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the read count data from Upton et al., shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In single-cell RC-seq samples, 53% of the 4049 calls of high-confidence gold-standard KNR insertions were detected with ≥3 reads per sample.
source: In single-cell RC-seq samples, 53%, 24% and 20% of the 4049 calls of high-confidence gold-standard KNR insertions were detected with ≥3, ≥20 and ≥40 reads per sample, respectively; only 32% were detected with only 1 read (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of KNR insertion read counts from Upton et al. data, shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In single-cell RC-seq samples, 24% of the 4049 calls of high-confidence gold-standard KNR insertions were detected with ≥20 reads per sample.
source: In single-cell RC-seq samples, 53%, 24% and 20% of the 4049 calls of high-confidence gold-standard KNR insertions were detected with ≥3, ≥20 and ≥40 reads per sample, respectively; only 32% were detected with only 1 read (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of KNR insertion read counts from Upton et al. data, shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In single-cell RC-seq samples, 20% of the 4049 calls of high-confidence gold-standard KNR insertions were detected with ≥40 reads per sample.
source: In single-cell RC-seq samples, 53%, 24% and 20% of the 4049 calls of high-confidence gold-standard KNR insertions were detected with ≥3, ≥20 and ≥40 reads per sample, respectively; only 32% were detected with only 1 read (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of KNR insertion read counts from Upton et al. data, shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In single-cell RC-seq samples, only 32% of high-confidence gold-standard KNR insertions were detected with only 1 read.
source: In single-cell RC-seq samples, 53%, 24% and 20% of the 4049 calls of high-confidence gold-standard KNR insertions were detected with ≥3, ≥20 and ≥40 reads per sample, respectively; only 32% were detected with only 1 read (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of KNR insertion read counts from Upton et al. data, shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only 0.4% (20/4759) of single-cell somatic insertion candidates were detected with ≥3 reads.
source: In contrast, 97% (4634/4759) of single-cell somatic insertion candidates were detected with only 1 read and only 0.4% (20/4759) with ≥3 reads (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of somatic candidate read counts from Upton et al., shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The strikingly higher read depths of gold-standard germline KNR L1 insertions relative to somatic insertion candidates in the same experiment is consistent with the vast majority of claimed somatic insertions not corresponding to bona fide insertions.
source: The strikingly higher read depths of gold-standard germline KNR L1 insertions relative to somatic insertion candidates in the same experiment is consistent with the vast majority of claimed somatic insertions not corresponding to bona fide insertions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of read count distributions.

claim: 11% of single-cell KNR insertion calls were detected at both L1 (5' and 3') junctions.
source: 11% of single-cell KNR insertion calls were detected at both L1 (5' and 3') junctions, whereas >250-fold less— only 0.04% (2/4682)— of single-cell somatic insertion candidates were detected at both junctions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of junction detection data from Upton et al., shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only 0.04% (2/4682) of single-cell somatic insertion candidates were detected at both junctions.
source: 11% of single-cell KNR insertion calls were detected at both L1 (5' and 3') junctions, whereas >250-fold less— only 0.04% (2/4682)— of single-cell somatic insertion candidates were detected at both junctions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of junction detection data from Upton et al., shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 8 of the 12 hippocampal single-cell somatic candidates detected at both junctions are chimera artifacts.
source: Sequence analysis shows 8 of the 12 hippocampal single-cell somatic candidates detected at both junctions (including candidates in which each junction was detected in a different sample) are chimera artifacts (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: RC-seq bulk somatic candidates have a non-canonical distribution of large TSD sizes, inconsistent with nearly all prior L1 research.
source: Furthermore, RC-seq bulk somatic candidates have a non-canonical distribution of large TSD sizes, inconsistent with nearly all prior L1 research (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TSD sizes in Appendix 1.

claim: Analysis of 10 randomly selected candidates with large (>50 bp) TSDs found all were chimera artifacts.
source: Analysis of 10 randomly selected candidates with large (>50 bp) TSDs found all were chimera artifacts (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: A read count threshold of > 2 optimizes sensitivity and specificity, maintaining detection of 53% of true positive KNR insertion calls across all single cells and a per-cell KNR detection sensitivity of 24%, while excluding ~99.6% of false-positive calls.
source: A read count threshold of > 2 optimizes sensitivity and specificity, maintaining detection of 53% of true positive KNR insertion calls across all single cells (Figure 2A) and a per-cell KNR detection sensitivity of 24% (Figure 3A), while excluding ~99.6% of false-positive calls (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on analysis of read count distributions and sensitivity calculations, shown in Figures 2A and 3A.

claim: Only 20 somatic insertion candidates supported by >2 reads were detected across all 170 cells.
source: Only 20 somatic insertion candidates supported by >2 reads were detected across all 170 cells, and 12 of these were chimeras upon further sequence analysis (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Upton et al. data with the >2 read threshold applied.

claim: 12 of the 20 somatic insertion candidates supported by >2 reads were chimeras upon further sequence analysis.
source: Only 20 somatic insertion candidates supported by >2 reads were detected across all 170 cells, and 12 of these were chimeras upon further sequence analysis (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The remaining 8 candidates yield a sensitivity-corrected somatic insertion rate estimate of 0.19 per cell.
source: The remaining 8 candidates yield a sensitivity-corrected somatic insertion rate estimate of 0.19 per cell, with no significant difference in rates between cell types (hippocampal neurons and glia, cortical neurons, and AGS hippocampal neurons) (p = 0.98, ANOVA) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on calculation using the 8 remaining candidates after filtering, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There is no significant difference in somatic insertion rates between cell types (hippocampal neurons and glia, cortical neurons, and AGS hippocampal neurons) (p = 0.98, ANOVA).
source: The remaining 8 candidates yield a sensitivity-corrected somatic insertion rate estimate of 0.19 per cell, with no significant difference in rates between cell types (hippocampal neurons and glia, cortical neurons, and AGS hippocampal neurons) (p = 0.98, ANOVA) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (ANOVA) of the rate data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 95% of single cells did not have any somatic insertion candidates (excluding chimeras) supported by >2 sequencing reads.
source: 95% of single cells did not have any somatic insertion candidates (excluding chimeras) supported by >2 sequencing reads.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the filtered candidate data.

claim: RC-seq somatic insertion rates are consistent with rates previously estimated by L1 insertion profiling (L1-IP) in single cortical and caudate neurons (0.07 ± 0.15 (SD); p = 0.54, ANOVA).
source: These RC-seq somatic insertion rates are quite consistent with rates previously estimated by L1 insertion profiling (L1-IP) in single cortical and caudate neurons (0.07 ± 0.15 (SD); p = 0.54, ANOVA) (Evrony et al., 2012), and using single-neuron whole-genome sequencing (0.18 ± 0.47 (SD); p = 0.37, ANOVA) (Evrony et al., 2015), suggesting a notable consensus by three methods confirming that somatic L1 insertions are present in human brain, but fewer than one per average genome.
evidence: This is based on comparison to prior studies and statistical analysis.

claim: RC-seq somatic insertion rates are consistent with rates estimated using single-neuron whole-genome sequencing (0.18 ± 0.47 (SD); p = 0.37, ANOVA).
source: These RC-seq somatic insertion rates are quite consistent with rates previously estimated by L1 insertion profiling (L1-IP) in single cortical and caudate neurons (0.07 ± 0.15 (SD); p = 0.54, ANOVA) (Evrony et al., 2012), and using single-neuron whole-genome sequencing (0.18 ± 0.47 (SD); p = 0.37, ANOVA) (Evrony et al., 2015), suggesting a notable consensus by three methods confirming that somatic L1 insertions are present in human brain, but fewer than one per average genome.
evidence: This is based on comparison to prior studies and statistical analysis.

claim: Three methods confirm that somatic L1 insertions are present in human brain, but fewer than one per average genome.
source: These RC-seq somatic insertion rates are quite consistent with rates previously estimated by L1 insertion profiling (L1-IP) in single cortical and caudate neurons (0.07 ± 0.15 (SD); p = 0.54, ANOVA) (Evrony et al., 2012), and using single-neuron whole-genome sequencing (0.18 ± 0.47 (SD); p = 0.37, ANOVA) (Evrony et al., 2015), suggesting a notable consensus by three methods confirming that somatic L1 insertions are present in human brain, but fewer than one per average genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of results across three different methods.

claim: 2 of the 8 somatic insertion candidates detected following read count filtering correspond to a single, likely bona fide L1Hs insertion in neuron #11 (12 reads) and glial cell #2 (6 reads) from the hippocampus of individual 45.
source: Notably, 2 of the 8 somatic insertion candidates detected following read count filtering correspond to a single, likely bona fide L1Hs insertion in neuron #11 (12 reads) and glial cell #2 (6 reads) from the hippocampus of individual 45 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: This intergenic insertion shows RC-seq reads capturing both 5' and 3' junctions bearing all the hallmarks of a true retrotransposition event: a TSD, poly-A tail, and a 3' transduction that traces its source to a population-polymorphic (KNR) L1 on chromosome 2 that was identified in a prior L1 profiling study.
source: This intergenic insertion shows RC-seq reads capturing both 5' and 3' junctions bearing all the hallmarks of a true retrotransposition event: a TSD, poly-A tail, and a 3' transduction that traces its source to a population-polymorphic (KNR) L1 on chromosome 2 that was identified in a prior L1 profiling study (Iskow et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the insertion and citation to a prior study.

claim: This same somatic insertion was also detected in glial cells #7 and #8 of the individual, each with 2 reads.
source: This same somatic insertion was also detected in glial cells #7 and #8 of the individual, each with 2 reads.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Upton et al. data.

claim: MALBAC-amplified single cells profiled by RC-seq had reduced performance relative to bulk RC-seq in terms of gold-standard KNR insertion read counts and junction detection rates.
source: MALBAC-amplified single cells profiled by RC-seq had reduced performance relative to bulk RC-seq in terms of gold-standard KNR insertion read counts and junction detection rates (Figures 2A–B), and had significantly lower sensitivity for KNR insertions (higher dropout) than L1 profiling of MDA-amplified single cells (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis shown in Figures 2A-B, 3A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MALBAC-amplified single cells had significantly lower sensitivity for KNR insertions (higher dropout) than L1 profiling of MDA-amplified single cells.
source: MALBAC-amplified single cells profiled by RC-seq had reduced performance relative to bulk RC-seq in terms of gold-standard KNR insertion read counts and junction detection rates (Figures 2A–B), and had significantly lower sensitivity for KNR insertions (higher dropout) than L1 profiling of MDA-amplified single cells (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At genomic scales < 50 kb, MALBAC-amplified single cells show systematic ~1 kb peaks of high genome amplification separated by troughs of low amplification or complete dropout.
source: Analysis of Upton et al.'s pre-RC-seq whole-genome sequencing of MALBAC-amplified single cells shows that at genomic scales < 50 kb (high-resolution view), which includes the size range of retrotransposons and single-nucleotide variants (SNV), there are systematic ~1 kb peaks of high genome amplification separated by troughs of low amplification or complete dropout (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: These peaks and troughs often occur in the same locations as in MALBAC single cells from an unrelated study by Zong et al. (2012), suggesting that this non-uniformity in genome amplification is inherent to MALBAC.
source: These peaks and troughs often occur in the same locations as in MALBAC single cells from an unrelated study by Zong et al. (2012) (Figure 4A), suggesting that this non-uniformity in genome amplification is inherent to MALBAC.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of MALBAC samples from different studies, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MDA single cells show significantly better uniformity of genome amplification at genomic scales < 50 kb than MALBAC single cells.
source: In contrast, MDA single cells show significantly better uniformity of genome amplification at these size scales (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The non-uniformity of MALBAC at genomic scales encompassing the size range of retrotransposon elements likely explains the subset of true KNR insertions appearing at low read counts and the low sensitivity (high allelic dropout) of single-cell RC-seq.
source: The non-uniformity of MALBAC at genomic scales encompassing the size range of retrotransposon elements likely explains the subset of true KNR insertions appearing at low read counts (Figure 2A) and the low sensitivity (high allelic dropout) of single-cell RC-seq (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed non-uniformity and its effects on detection.

claim: MALBAC's non-uniformity explains MALBAC's lower overall breadth of genome-wide coverage at nucleotide resolution (i.e. higher locus dropout) relative to MDA.
source: It also explains MALBAC's lower overall breadth of genome-wide coverage at nucleotide resolution (i.e. higher locus dropout) relative to MDA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the non-uniformity analysis, with data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Individual MALBAC single cells from Upton et al. have significantly lower quality than both MALBAC single cells from Zong et al. and MDA single neurons at genomic scales of ~500 kb bins.
source: At larger genomic scales of ~500 kb bins (low-resolution view), MALBAC single cells from Upton et al. show significantly lower quality and higher variability among individual cells than both MALBAC-amplified single cells from Zong et al. and MDA-amplified single neurons (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Pooling of all 92 normal hippocampus single neurons from Upton et al. shows performance commensurate with MALBAC single cells from Zong et al., indicating that the low quality of Upton et al.'s single cells may be due to stochastic factors preceding MALBAC, such as poor tissue quality, rather than MALBAC itself.
source: Pooling of all 92 normal hippocampus single neurons from Upton et al. shows performance commensurate with MALBAC single cells from Zong et al. (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B), indicating that the low quality of Upton et al.'s single cells may be due to stochastic factors preceding MALBAC, such as poor tissue quality, rather than MALBAC itself.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pooled sample analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: At genomic scales of ~500 kb bins, MALBAC single cells from Zong et al. have high reproducibility and better uniformity of genome coverage than MDA.
source: Of note, at these genomic scales, MALBAC single cells from Zong et al. have high reproducibility and better uniformity of genome coverage than MDA (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B) (Evrony et al., 2015), enabling MALBAC's better performance in detection of large copy number variants (Hou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B, and supported by citations.

claim: MALBAC enables better performance in detection of large copy number variants.
source: Of note, at these genomic scales, MALBAC single cells from Zong et al. have high reproducibility and better uniformity of genome coverage than MDA (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B) (Evrony et al., 2015), enabling MALBAC's better performance in detection of large copy number variants (Hou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hou et al., 2013.

claim: Power spectral density measuring amplification uniformity across all genomic scales confirmed better uniformity of MALBAC at large genomic scales (> 30 kb) and better uniformity of MDA at small genomic scales (< 30 kb).
source: Power spectral density measuring amplification uniformity across all genomic scales confirmed better uniformity of MALBAC at large genomic scales (> 30 kb) and better uniformity of MDA at small genomic scales (< 30 kb) (Figure 4C) (Evrony et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on power spectral density analysis shown in Figure 4C, supported by citations.

claim: MALBAC and MDA each have advantages at different genomic scales and for different mutation types.
source: Altogether, these results: a) suggest MALBAC and low quality single cells as contributors to single-cell RC-seq sensitivity loss; b) emphasize the importance of single-cell quality control at genomic scales relevant to the studied mutation type; and c) confirm that MALBAC and MDA each have advantages at different genomic scales and for different mutation types but that MALBAC is not especially well-suited for retrotransposon studies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparative analyses presented.

claim: MALBAC is not especially well-suited for retrotransposon studies.
source: Altogether, these results: a) suggest MALBAC and low quality single cells as contributors to single-cell RC-seq sensitivity loss; b) emphasize the importance of single-cell quality control at genomic scales relevant to the studied mutation type; and c) confirm that MALBAC and MDA each have advantages at different genomic scales and for different mutation types but that MALBAC is not especially well-suited for retrotransposon studies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analyses showing MALBAC's limitations at the genomic scales relevant to retrotransposons.

claim: L1 mosaicism is not "ubiquitous" in the hippocampus.
source: Here, we have shown that L1 mosaicism is not "ubiquitous" in the hippocampus and that somatic insertion rates in the recent paper by Upton et al. were elevated > 50-fold due to the informatic analysis and a lack of definitive validation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the reanalysis showing much lower rates than Upton et al. reported.

claim: Somatic insertion rates in Upton et al. were elevated > 50-fold due to the informatic analysis and a lack of definitive validation.
source: Here, we have shown that L1 mosaicism is not "ubiquitous" in the hippocampus and that somatic insertion rates in the recent paper by Upton et al. were elevated > 50-fold due to the informatic analysis and a lack of definitive validation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the reanalysis identifying artifacts and methodological issues.

claim: The corrected rate of retrotransposition is consistent with prior single-cell studies.
source: Reanalysis of their data while filtering these artifacts generates a consensus that retrotransposition does occur in developing brain but at a much lower rate consistent with prior single-cell studies (Evrony et al., 2012; Evrony et al., 2015), thereby constraining the range of possible functional roles for retrotransposition in the brain.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the corrected rate to prior studies.

claim: The corrected RC-seq retrotransposition rate is consistent with rates measured in vitro in neuronal progenitors.
source: The corrected RC-seq retrotransposition rate is significant as it aligns to a wholly different regime of potential functional roles for retrotransposition in the brain (rare normal variation and rare disease) rather than a "ubiquitous" role. This corrected rate is consistent with rates measured in vitro in neuronal progenitors (Coufal et al., 2009) and is consistent with the absence of significant somatic L1 insertions in brain tumors (Helman et al., 2014; Iskow et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on comparison to prior in vitro studies, supported by citation.

claim: The corrected rate is consistent with the absence of significant somatic L1 insertions in brain tumors.
source: The corrected RC-seq retrotransposition rate is significant as it aligns to a wholly different regime of potential functional roles for retrotransposition in the brain (rare normal variation and rare disease) rather than a "ubiquitous" role. This corrected rate is consistent with rates measured in vitro in neuronal progenitors (Coufal et al., 2009) and is consistent with the absence of significant somatic L1 insertions in brain tumors (Helman et al., 2014; Iskow et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on comparison to brain tumor studies, supported by citations.

claim: Chimeric DNA molecules falsely linking unrelated DNA fragments are well known to arise during single-cell genome amplification.
source: Although whole genome amplification methods have remarkable abilities to amplify picogram quantities of DNA from a single cell into microgram quantities, chimeric DNA molecules falsely linking unrelated DNA fragments are well known to arise during single-cell genome amplification (Macaulay and Voet, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about single-cell amplification, supported by citation.

claim: Chimera artifacts arise during ligation and PCR steps of sequencing library preparation.
source: Chimera artifacts also arise during ligation and PCR steps of sequencing library preparation (Kircher et al., 2012; Quail et al., 2008), processes integral to the RC-seq method.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sequencing library preparation, supported by citations.

claim: Chimeric sequences can create a DNA fragment connecting a LINE element to an unrelated portion of the genome, creating the appearance of biological LINE mobilization.
source: Chimeric sequences can create a DNA fragment connecting a LINE element to an unrelated portion of the genome, creating the appearance of biological LINE mobilization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is an inference about how chimeras can create false-positive L1 calls, illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.
